title: Catch Me If You Can
full_review:
In Steven Spielberg's fact-based crime comedy "Catch Me If You Can" (DreamWorks), a 16-year-old fleeing his divorcing parents sets himself up as a doctor, a lawyer and an airline pilot. In the process he (Leonardo DiCaprio) cashes millions of dollars in fraudulent checks over several years, attracting the attention of the FBI and one particular agent (Tom Hanks) determined to nail the cocky culprit.

Based on Frank Abagnale Jr.'s same-titled 1980 autobiography, the film's breezy tone treats the teen's felonies as a lark, but eventually the relationship between the thief and the agent develops along the lines of redemptive possibilities.

Frank is first seen playing the impostor in 1963 when he transfers to a new school where he is assumed to be the substitute French teacher. Game for the jest, he goes for it and a week later when he is found out his morally lax father (Christopher Walken) just laughs. Frank idolizes his father and when he's told his unfaithful French mother (Nathalie Baye) is divorcing his dad, Frank is traumatized and runs away.

Noticing how people look up to airline pilots, he fakes his way into getting a Pan Am pilot's uniform, and begins creating valid-looking checks by flirting with bank tellers and learning inside industry tricks of the trade. A quick study, he devises ingenious ways to avoid detection, but FBI special agent Carl Hanratty (Hanks) is nothing if not patient in trying to identify and catch the elusive check-kiter.

Meanwhile, adolescent Frank is living the high life in Atlanta as a phony pilot, with girls at his beck and call. When he realizes Hanratty is getting close he simply changes professions, transforming into an emergency-room physician where he falls for candy-striper Brenda (Amy Adams). In New Orleans Frank persuades her attorney father (Martin Sheen) that he's also a lawyer willing to work with his future father-in-law. His medical and legal training consists of watching "Perry Mason" and doctor dramas.

Hanratty, however, is closing in, and realizing Frank is not truly an adult, wants to arrest him peacefully and perhaps be instrumental in his rehabilitation. Frank himself doesn't question his morals, but this is where the movie has a positive outlook. Despite treating Frank's crimes as admirably clever, the film acknowledges that he must pay for his behavior, and shows how a person is capable of change and can start anew, especially with the support of generous mentor Hanratty, whom Frank had made a fool of several times in the past.

DiCaprio carries off his role with an easy panache while Hanks gives an unusually quirky performance as the dogged bureaucrat who won't rest until he both collars and converts his man.

The film lags in spots but the high-style period visuals, especially the cars, costumes and coiffures, are a hoot, bound to hold nostalgic appeal for baby-boomers. Walken also delivers in an underwritten role with a slippery performance as a father whose lax ethics may have inspired his son to try deception as a way of life. Always seeking the approval of his father, Frank eventually seems to transfer his need for a father figure to the very man who is determined to lock him up, but with unexpected results that give the film an upbeat bounce at the end.

Because of light-hearted treatment of crime, implied sexual encounters, an abortion reference, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
